summary: Relict: Field Archive – Abandoned, Not Forgotten is an interactive web experience that turns space-mission history into stories for school-age explorers. Spacecraft, rovers, landers and instruments are often left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Our Field Archive lets students meet these machines, learn what each one did, why it stayed, and what science it made possible, using real NASA mission records and images. A built-in quiz helps students check what they learned. By giving forgotten hardware a story, Relict helps young people feel a personal connection to past missions and shows how the science from them paves the way for future exploration.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Relict: Field Archive – Abandoned, Not Forgotten is an interactive web archive that tells the stories of NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Students begin at Earth and open 12 field records across three exploration domains, covering 58 years from Surveyor 1 in 1966 to Ingenuity in 2024. Each record is a short mission dossier covering what the machine was, why it was sent, how it ended and what science it left behind. The archive includes the Apollo ALSEP science stations and Lunar Roving Vehicles, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, Dawn and Ingenuity.

HOW IT WORKS

The page is a guided scroll. Students choose a signal to open a program dossier, then explore a section on how engineering choices made discovery possible: purpose, engineering lesson and science return. A "Beyond the warranty" chart compares planned and actual lifetimes, such as Opportunity's 90 planned sols versus 5,111 achieved. Mission pictures come from the NASA Image and Video Library, and every record links to a NASA source. A 10-question knowledge check ends the journey, and students earn a Space Historian badge, or Mission Commander for a perfect score.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Most students only hear about active missions. Relict gives retired spacecraft a story, so young people see them as explorers rather than debris. It also shows why hardware is left behind and how a finished mission still produces knowledge. Our aim is to inspire school-age and casual space fans and connect engineering to science.

WHAT WE USED

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the NASA Image and Video Library API, NASA mission pages and archives as sources, and Google Fonts .

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

The experience is framed as a field archive, with coordinates, dossiers and a badge system, instead of a list of facts. Slide visuals and the site share one visual language of dark space, mission colors and short, story-led text.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy, by tying each record to a NASA source. Audience, with plain language for school-age readers. Accessibility, with readable type and support for reduced-motion settings. Balance, by covering both deliberate abandonment, such as parked rovers, and missions that ended through failure or loss of power.
